newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians sceptical of fast recovery for Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Russians sceptical of fast recovery for Yeltsin.

text.p: Muscovites were sceptical on Wednesday of President Boris Yeltsin's chances of a speedy recovery from heart surgery despite a deluge of positive comments from Kremlin officials and heart specialists.
"It's not going to be very easy for him to come back to work," said Alexander, a grizzled traffic inspector of 43. "He'll probably be out of things for a year."

"They say he's got up and he's talking but we don't know anything more than that," said Lena, 44, selling newspapers and pornographic magazines from a small kiosk as Muscovites went to work on a grey morning.

Yeltsin's announcement on television on September 5 that he planned to have the operation marked a breach in the Kremlin wall of silence which has for centuries kept curiosity about the health of its occupants at bay.

But ordinary Russians, long accustomed to a fog of disinformation on the true state of health of their leaders, took reports that Yeltsin had bounced back only a day after major open-heart surgery with a pinch of salt.
The Kremlin said that on Wednesday morning Yeltsin came off his lung-machine, took back his presidential powers and was pronounced in "satisfactory" condition by doctors, pleased at his progress.
But there were still no pictures of Yeltsin on Russian television, the most influential medium in the vast country of some 150 million people.

U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, the pioneer of bypass surgery and an observer at Yeltsin's operation, went further, telling CNN television the president could be playing his beloved tennis again in three or four months.
"Within three or four months he could do almost anything he wants," he said.
The wide-circulation daily Izvestia took a similar approach, declaring in a headline: "We congratulate the president and the doctors."
After months of speculation over the state of Yeltsin's health, the newspaper wrote in dizzy tones of the Kremlin's new-found openness.
"The operation on Boris Yeltsin's heart began on November 5 at 7 a.m. and already in just a few minutes the Kremlin press service gave its first piece of information," Izvestia said.

Vyacheslav, 43, selling reams of photocopying paper under a small blue and white striped tent on a pavement in central Moscow, said Yeltsin was physically no longer up to the job of running the crisis-prone country.
"Unfortunately, his health is still not up to the situation in the country," he said. "It would be better if someone else was president for this difficult time but there is no clear candidate."
